Short answer: NAD(P) binding is not a marker of a single common ancestor. It is a functional trait that evolved by both divergent and convergent routes, and SCOPe keeps the groups apart on that basis.

Divergent evolution: Within a single SCOPe superfamily, NAD(P) binding is usually inherited from a common ancestor. The clearest case is the very large Rossmann-type superfamily c.2.1 "NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains" (SUNID 51735) in fold c.2 (SUNID 51734), class c (alpha/beta). Its members include dehydrogenases and reductases such as alcohol dehydrogenase catalytic-domain partners (e.g., d1uufa2, d1vj0a2), the SDR-like domains and others. They have diverged in substrate, chemistry and sequence while keeping the dinucleotide-binding core. Homology there is supported by structure, conserved cofactor-binding motifs and shared architecture, not by the cofactor alone. These are SCOPe release 2.08 facts.

Convergent evolution: NAD(P)-binding enzymes also appear in other, separately classified folds and superfamilies. One example is c.3.1 "FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain" (SUNID 51905) in fold c.3 (SUNID 51904), which is a different fold and superfamily from c.2.1 in the same class c. Other NAD(P)-using enzymes fall in unrelated folds, such as some TIM-barrel and other alpha/beta folds, and in other classes. The existence of these separate groupings implies that no single ancestor accounts for all NAD(P) binding. Where the folds differ, the best-supported explanation is independent origins that converged on a similar function (binding an adenine-ribose-pyrophosphate-nicotinamide ligand), or, at most, a very remote relationship that cannot be shown. SCOPe treats these as distinct folds and superfamilies. Separation at the fold or superfamily level is a statement that homology has not been demonstrated; it is not proof of independent origin.

Why cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone is insufficient evidence of homology:
1. Function does not equal ancestry. Binding the same ligand can be achieved by unrelated folds. A shared ligand constrains the active site, so unrelated proteins can arrive at similar features, such as a glycine-rich loop, an acidic residue that binds the ribose hydroxyls, or similar catalytic residues.
2. Small motifs are weak evidence. A short motif such as a GxGxxG pattern can arise by chance or by convergence, and a similar active-site layout in unrelated scaffolds says nothing about the rest of the structure.
3. Homology is an inference about common ancestry. It needs support from significant sequence similarity, or from overall structural similarity beyond the ligand-binding site (matching topology and strand order, conserved core, shared sequence or structural features, and functional links among intermediates). Structural similarity of only part of a domain, such as the nucleotide-binding half, is not sufficient.
4. Fold sharing is not homology either. In SCOPe a shared fold, even by FATCAT or other structure matches, is not by itself homology, and differing folds do not prove non-homology. The superfamily level is the one that asserts probable common ancestry. The family level indicates clearer relationships.
5. Function transfer and template use are risky. Do not assume that two proteins that bind NAD(P) share an ancestor, mechanism, substrate or classification, and do not use one as a template for the other without sequence or structural evidence of homology at the relevant region. The classification of a reference domain does not automatically apply to a different protein.

Conclusion: NAD(P)-binding enzymes are best described as a case where divergent evolution explains the large within-superfamily radiations (c.2.1) and convergent evolution (or unproven relationships) explains why the trait recurs in other folds and superfamilies (e.g., c.3.1). Homology claims must rest on sequence and overall structure evidence, not on shared cofactor or active-site features.
